source.title: Interest in Disguise
source.summary: Tawarruq, hiyal, and the uncomfortable question: do Islamic banks truly avoid riba?
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: A customer walks into an Islamic bank wanting a loan. The bank buys metal on the London exchange, sells it to the customer at a markup, the customer immediately sells the metal back to the market at a loss, and walks out with cash. The metal never moved. No one wanted the metal. The entire transaction existed to disguise what was, economically, an interest-bearing loan. This is tawarruq, and it accounts for a significant portion of Islamic banking transactions globally. This episode confronts the most uncomfortable debate in modern Islamic finance: when legal tricks (hiyal) replicate the economic substance of riba, have we honored the spirit of the prohibition or merely its letter? Scholars like Mufti Taqi Usmani have called organized tawarruq impermissible, yet the practice continues to grow.

x.single_post: Most people think Islamic banks avoid interest by using different contracts. They actually use legal tricks to replicate the same economic outcome. A bank buys metal, sells it to you at markup, you sell it back at a loss. The metal never moves.
